chapter.name: The Beginnings of Indian Civilisation
chapter.blurb: The Indus, Harappan or Sindhu-Sarasvati civilisation, one of the world's oldest, grew from villages into planned cities from about 3500 BCE, reaching its peak between roughly 2600 and 1900 BCE. Its cities show precise town-planning, sophisticated water management (the Great Bath, wells and Dholavira's reservoirs), varied agriculture including the first cotton-growing in Eurasia, and a brisk internal and maritime trade reaching as far as Iran and Oman. Around 1900 BCE the civilisation began to decline, most likely due to climatic change and the Sarasvati river drying up, not warfare; its people gradually returned to rural life, carrying much of its culture forward into later Indian civilisation.

scope_in.item: A civilisation is defined as an advanced stage of human society with at least seven characteristics: government/administration, urbanism (town-planning, water management, drainage), a variety of crafts, trade (internal and external), a form of writing, cultural ideas (art, architecture, literature, oral traditions, social customs), and a productive agriculture; civilisation began at different times in different regions of the world, starting with Mesopotamia (about 3500 BCE) and Egypt (about 3100 BCE), before the Indus-Sarasvati civilisation (about 2600-1900 BCE)

From about 3500 BCE, villages in the Indus and Sarasvati river plains grew into towns, and around 2600 BCE those towns grew into cities -- India's 'First Urbanisation'; the civilisation is called by several names (Indus, Harappan, Indus-Sarasvati, Sindhu-Sarasvati), its people are called Harappans (after Harappa, in Pakistan's Punjab, excavated 1920-21 and identified in 1924); the once-used term 'Indus Valley civilisation' is now considered obsolete since sites extend well beyond the Indus valley; the Sarasvati river, first mentioned in the Rig Veda, is today's seasonal Ghaggar-Hakra river; major cities include Harappa (Punjab, Pakistan), Mohenjo-daro (Sindh, Pakistan), Dholavira (Gujarat), Rakhigarhi (Haryana), Kalibangan (Rajasthan) and Ganweriwala (Cholistan desert, Pakistan)

Harappan cities were built to precise plans, with wide streets often oriented to the cardinal directions, fortifications, and two distinct parts -- an 'upper town' for the local elite and a 'lower town' for common people; buildings were generally made of brick, of similar construction quality regardless of house size; the Great Bath at Mohenjo-daro (about 12 x 7 metres, waterproofed with natural bitumen) is a famous structure whose exact purpose remains debated, though it was probably not a general public bath since individual houses had their own bathrooms; drains ran below streets; Mohenjo-daro had about 700 brick wells; Dholavira had at least six large reservoirs cut into rock, connected by underground drains, the largest measuring 73 metres in length

Harappan settlements were often built along riverbanks for water access and fertile soil; they grew cereals (barley, wheat, some millets, sometimes rice), pulses and vegetables, and were the first in Eurasia to grow cotton, used for weaving cloth; they used farming tools including the plough; they domesticated animals for meat and fished in rivers and the sea; scientific study of cooking-pot residues found dairy products, turmeric, ginger and banana; cities depended on a steady daily supply of produce from surrounding rural villages

The Harappans conducted active internal and external trade by land, river and sea routes, exporting ornaments, timber, and other everyday objects, and probably gold and cotton; carnelian beads (from a stone found mostly in Gujarat) and conch-shell bangles were prized crafted exports; they mastered copper-working and, by adding tin, produced the harder metal bronze, used for tools, pots, pans and figurines; the huge basin at Lothal (217 m long, 36 m wide) is believed to be a dockyard, evidence of the first intensive maritime activity in India; thousands of small steatite seals, bearing animal figures and an as-yet undeciphered writing system, likely helped identify traders and goods; Harappan carnelian beads have been found at Susa (Iran) and an ivory comb on the coast of Oman

Archaeological finds reveal Harappan daily life and culture, including objects of daily use (a bronze mirror, terracotta pots, stone weights, a bronze chisel, a gamesboard, a terracotta whistle) and cultural/symbolic objects (a statuette often called the 'Priest King', though its identity is not actually known; a seal showing a swastika; the Pashupati Seal, showing a three-faced deity surrounded by animals; the bronze 'Dancing Girl' figurine from Mohenjo-daro; a Lothal pot design resembling the story of a thirsty crow); around 1900 BCE the Sindhu-Sarasvati civilisation began to fall apart, cities were abandoned, and people gradually adopted a rural lifestyle; two agreed factors are a climatic change causing reduced rainfall from about 2200 BCE onward, and the Sarasvati river drying up in its central basin (abandoning cities such as Kalibangan and Banawali); there is no evidence of warfare or invasion; much Harappan culture and technology survived into the next phase of Indian civilisation

concepts.name: What is a civilisation?
concepts.description: A civilisation is an advanced stage of human society with at least seven characteristics, and it began at different times in different parts of the world.
concepts.idea: A civilisation is an advanced stage of human society, marked by at least seven characteristics: government and administration, urbanism, a variety of crafts, trade, writing, cultural ideas, and productive agriculture.
concepts.rule: Civilisation began at different times in different parts of the world -- Mesopotamia (about 3500 BCE), then Egypt (about 3100 BCE), and later the Indus-Sarasvati civilisation (about 2600 to 1900 BCE).
concepts.example: The seven characteristics listed in the chapter include government/administration, urbanism (town-planning, water management, drainage), a variety of crafts, trade (internal and external), a form of writing, cultural ideas expressed through art/architecture/literature, and productive agriculture.

questions.q: Using the chapter's seven characteristics of civilisation, design a short checklist (at least five items) that an archaeologist could use in the field to judge whether a newly excavated ancient settlement was part of a 'civilisation.'
questions.a: Sample checklist: (1) Is there evidence of a government or administration, such as large public buildings? (2) Is there evidence of town-planning, such as streets, drains or fortifications? (3) Are there signs of specialised crafts, such as workshops or tools? (4) Is there evidence of trade, such as imported materials or standard weights? (5) Is there any form of writing, such as inscribed seals? (6) Is there evidence of productive agriculture, such as stored grain or farming tools?
s: Lists at least five checklist items, each tied to a distinct named characteristic
Each item names a concrete kind of archaeological evidence, not just the characteristic's name repeated
Checklist is usable in the field, i.e. describes observable evidence rather than abstract ideas

questions.q: The chapter says the term 'civilisation' describes 'an advanced stage of human societies.' Which of these best explains what makes a stage 'advanced' in the chapter's sense?
questions.a: The presence of organised features like government, urbanism, crafts, trade, writing and culture together, not any single feature alone
o: The presence of organised features like government, urbanism, crafts, trade, writing and culture together, not any single feature alone
Simply having a very large population
Simply living in a hot climate

questions.q: Consider: (I) According to the chapter, civilisation began in Mesopotamia before it began in the Indus-Sarasvati region. (II) According to the chapter, a civilisation must have writing as its only defining characteristic. Which is or are correct?
questions.a: Only I

questions.q: The chapter lists 'a productive agriculture' as a characteristic of civilisation, not simply 'agriculture.' Explain why the word 'productive' matters here.
questions.a: Simply growing some food is not enough; the farming has to produce more than the farmers themselves need, a surplus, so that it can also feed people living in towns and cities who are not growing their own food; without that surplus, cities could not exist.
s: Explains that 'productive' means producing a surplus beyond the farmers' own needs
Connects this surplus to the ability to feed non-farming town/city populations

questions.q: A classmate claims, 'Writing is the single most important characteristic of civilisation -- without it, none of the others matter.' Evaluate this claim using the chapter's list of seven characteristics.
questions.a: This claim overstates writing's importance. The chapter lists seven characteristics -- government, urbanism, crafts, trade, writing, cultural ideas and agriculture -- as working together, not writing alone; for example, the chapter treats farming productivity as essential too, since without enough food, no city could support specialised crafts or trade, whether or not writing existed. Writing is important, especially for record-keeping and communication, but the chapter presents all seven as jointly necessary rather than ranking one above the rest.
s: States that the claim overstates or is not fully supported
Explains that the chapter lists seven characteristics together, not one as most important
Gives a specific reason another characteristic, e.g. agriculture, is also essential

questions.q: Invent a short 'Big Questions' style opening for a chapter about a possible future or imaginary civilisation you design yourself, listing at least three of its own characteristics inspired by, but different in detail from, the seven listed in this chapter.
questions.a: Sample: Big Questions -- 1. What is 'Skyharbour civilisation'? 2. How did its people manage floating cities? 3. What made its trade special? Description: Skyharbour civilisation has (1) a council-based government coordinating floating platforms, (2) urbanism in the form of interlinked floating city-platforms with their own water-recycling systems, and (3) trade in engineered materials carried by airship between platforms.
s: Provides at least three clearly stated 'Big Questions' or an equivalent framing
Includes at least three distinct invented characteristics, each clearly inspired by a named chapter characteristic
The invented civilisation is internally consistent, not contradicting its own stated characteristics

concepts.name: Names, geography and origins of the Indus-Sarasvati civilisation
concepts.description: Villages in the Indus-Sarasvati river plains grew into cities from about 3500-2600 BCE, and the resulting civilisation carries several names, reflecting both its rivers and its discovery history.
concepts.idea: Villages in the Indus and Sarasvati river plains grew into towns from about 3500 BCE, and those towns grew into cities around 2600 BCE -- India's 'First Urbanisation'; the resulting civilisation has several names.
concepts.rule: The civilisation is called 'Indus', 'Harappan', 'Indus-Sarasvati' or 'Sindhu-Sarasvati'; its people are called 'Harappans' after Harappa, the first site excavated (1920-21) and identified (1924); the older term 'Indus Valley civilisation' is now considered obsolete because sites extend far beyond the Indus valley; the Sarasvati river of the Rig Veda is today's seasonal Ghaggar-Hakra river.
concepts.example: Harappa (Punjab, Pakistan) and Mohenjo-daro (Sindh, Pakistan) were the first two cities identified, in 1924; later major cities discovered include Dholavira (Gujarat), Rakhigarhi (Haryana), Kalibangan (Rajasthan) and Ganweriwala (Cholistan desert, Pakistan).

questions.q: A textbook diagram lists both 'Harappan' and 'Indus-Sarasvati' as names for the same civilisation. Explain why a civilisation that grew up mainly along the Indus river also carries the name of a second river, the Sarasvati.
questions.a: Many important Harappan sites, including major cities like Rakhigarhi and Kalibangan, were found not along the Indus but along the Sarasvati river system (today's seasonal Ghaggar-Hakra); since so many sites belong to the Sarasvati basin as well as the Indus, the name 'Indus-Sarasvati' (or 'Sindhu-Sarasvati') recognises both rivers rather than just one.
s: States that many major sites were found along the Sarasvati/Ghaggar-Hakra basin, not just the Indus
Explains that naming both rivers reflects this shared geography

questions.q: Using the place names given in the chapter, plan a short 'discovery timeline' of at least three dated or ordered events in how this civilisation came to be known and named, from its first excavation to how we refer to it today.
questions.a: Sample timeline: (1) 1920-21: Harappa, in Punjab (Pakistan), is excavated for the first time. (2) 1924: Harappa and Mohenjo-daro are identified as belonging to a previously unknown ancient civilisation. (3) Because Harappa was excavated first, the civilisation is named 'Harappan'; because sites were later found across the wider Indus and Sarasvati river systems, not just the Indus valley, it also comes to be called the 'Indus-Sarasvati' or 'Sindhu-Sarasvati' civilisation, and the older term 'Indus Valley civilisation' becomes considered obsolete.
s: Correctly places excavation (1920-21) and identification (1924) in order
Explains why the civilisation is called 'Harappan'
Explains why 'Indus Valley civilisation' became an obsolete/replaced name

questions.a: Only I

questions.q: Harappa was excavated first, in 1920-21, yet the chapter says its identification as belonging to an unknown civilisation goes back to 1924. Explain why these could be two different dates for related events.
questions.a: Excavating a site (1920-21) means physically digging it up and finding objects and structures, which is a different step from recognising and publicly identifying what has been found as evidence of a previously unknown, ancient civilisation (1924); archaeologists needed time after the dig to study, compare and interpret the finds before announcing this conclusion.
s: Distinguishes excavation as physically digging up/finding objects
Explains identification as a later step of interpreting and announcing what the finds meant

questions.a: This claim is not supported by the chapter. questions.q: Invent a short museum information-plaque, in your own words, that explains to visitors why this ancient Indian civilisation has several different names, using at least three of the names given in the chapter.
questions.a: Sample plaque: 'Several names for one civilisation. All these names describe the same remarkable people.'
s: Names and correctly explains at least three of the chapter's names for the civilisation
Gives the correct reason behind at least one name, e.g. Harappan from Harappa's excavation
Written in a museum-plaque style accessible to a general visitor

concepts.name: Town-planning and water management
concepts.description: Harappan cities were built to precise plans, with organised streets, fortifications, and sophisticated water management including the Great Bath, wells and Dholavira's reservoirs.
concepts.idea: Harappan cities were built to precise plans -- wide streets oriented to cardinal directions, fortifications, and two distinct parts, the 'upper town' for the elite and the 'lower town' for common people.
concepts.rule: Cities had drains running below streets to carry away waste water; individual houses of all sizes were built to the same quality, generally in brick; the Great Bath at Mohenjo-daro (about 12 x 7 m, waterproofed with bitumen) is a famous, still-debated structure; Dholavira had at least six large reservoirs cut into rock, the largest measuring 73 m in length, connected by underground drains.

questions.q: The chapter says the purpose of the Great Bath 'remains a matter of debate,' even though the idea of it being an ordinary public bath is ruled out. Explain why archaeologists can rule out one explanation while still not being certain of the true purpose.
questions.a: Ruling out an explanation, such as 'a bath for the general public,' only needs one piece of contradicting evidence -- here, that most houses already had their own bathrooms, making a shared public bath less likely; but confirming which of the remaining explanations, such as a royal bath or a ritual tank, is the true one needs stronger direct evidence, like written records or clear symbolic markings, which have not been found.
s: Explains that ruling out one explanation needs only contradicting evidence, which exists here
Explains that confirming the true purpose among remaining options needs stronger, currently missing evidence

questions.q: A classmate says, 'Harappan cities must have had no rules or planning at all, since we cannot read anything they wrote.' Evaluate this claim using evidence from the chapter.
questions.a: This claim is not supported by the chapter's evidence. Even without being able to read Harappan writing, the physical remains show extensive planning: wide streets oriented to cardinal directions, city-wide underground drainage, fortifications, division into upper and lower towns, and coordinated structures like the Great Bath and Dholavira's connected reservoirs. All of this points to organised administration and rules governing construction and water management, even though we cannot read any written laws directly.
s: States the claim is not supported
Names at least two specific physical pieces of planning evidence from the chapter
Explains that this evidence implies organisation/rules even without readable writing

questions.q: Imagine you are guiding a school group through a reconstructed Harappan city. Write a short guided-tour script (at least three stops) describing what visitors would see, based on details in the chapter.
questions.a: Sample script: 'Stop 1: Here is the upper town, where the local elite likely lived, protected by this fortification wall. Stop 2: Notice these wide streets running exactly north-south and east-west -- Harappan planners built to a precise grid. Stop 3: This is the Great Bath, about 12 by 7 metres, waterproofed with natural bitumen; small rooms surround it, and a drain lets it be emptied and refilled. Notice most houses nearby also have their own private bathroom, connected to the drains running beneath the street.'
s: Includes at least three distinct, clearly described stops
Each stop correctly uses a specific fact from the chapter (dimensions, materials, layout, etc.)
Script reads as a coherent guided tour, not a disconnected list of facts

concepts.name: Crafts and trade: a brisk trade
concepts.description: The Harappans engaged in active internal and external trade, exporting crafted goods, and their steatite seals likely helped identify traders and goods.
concepts.idea: The Harappans engaged in active internal and external trade, exporting goods such as ornaments, timber and cotton, and specialising in crafts such as bead-making, shell-working and metalworking.
concepts.rule: Copper, a soft metal, could be combined with tin to make bronze, a harder metal used for tools, pots, pans and figurines; carnelian beads and conch-shell bangles were prized crafted exports; Lothal's huge basin (217 m long, 36 m wide) is believed to be a dockyard, evidence of the first intensive maritime activity in India; thousands of small steatite seals, carrying animal figures and an undeciphered writing system, likely helped identify traders and their goods.
concepts.example: Harappan carnelian beads have been found at Susa (in present-day Iran); an ivory comb (about 7 cm long) has been found on the coast of Oman, showing how far Harappan trade reached.

concepts.name: Art, everyday life and the decline of the civilisation
concepts.description: Archaeological finds reveal Harappan daily life and culture, and despite its achievements the civilisation gradually declined and its cities were abandoned.
concepts.idea: Archaeological finds (tools, games, ornaments, seals and figurines) reveal Harappan daily life and culture; despite its achievements, the civilisation gradually declined and its cities were abandoned.
concepts.rule: Cultural/symbolic objects include the 'Priest King' statuette (whose identity is not actually known), a seal showing a swastika, the Pashupati Seal (a three-faced deity surrounded by animals), and the bronze 'Dancing Girl' figurine from Mohenjo-daro; the civilisation began to fall apart around 1900 BCE; two agreed factors are climatic change (a drier phase from about 2200 BCE) and the drying up of the Sarasvati river's central basin (abandoning cities like Kalibangan and Banawali); there is no evidence of warfare or invasion, and people gradually adopted a rural lifestyle.
concepts.example: The design on a pot from Lothal seems to tell the story of the thirsty crow, remembered for more than 4,000 years; much of Harappan culture and technology survived and passed on to the next phase of Indian civilisation.

questions.q: Design a short museum exhibit label (at least four sentences) titled 'Why Did the Cities Empty?', summarising the chapter's explanation of the civilisation's decline for young visitors.

questions.q: A classmate claims, 'The Harappan civilisation just disappeared completely and left nothing behind.' Evaluate this claim using the chapter.
questions.a: This claim is not accurate. While Harappan cities were indeed abandoned around 1900 BCE due to climatic change and the Sarasvati river drying up, the chapter explicitly states that much of the Harappan culture and technology survived and was passed on to the next phase of Indian civilisation. So the civilisation's cities ended, but its influence did not simply vanish -- it continued in altered form, which is why the chapter titles this section 'The End or a New Beginning?' rather than simply 'The End.'
s: States that the claim is not accurate/is overstated
Correctly explains that culture and technology survived into the next phase of Indian civilisation
